analysis.one_liner: Taxes big oil companies' windfall profits at 50% and rebates the money to taxpayers as gasoline-price credits.
analysis.headline: Introduced in March 2026 with 14 Senate supporters and referred to the Senate Finance Committee, which has taken no action on it.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill puts a 50% excise tax on the profits large oil companies make when crude oil prices rise above their 2025 average level. It applies only to companies that extract or import more than 300,000 barrels a day. The money collected goes into a fund and is paid back to individual taxpayers as a credit on their taxes, phasing out for households earning over $150,000.
analysis.who_benefits: Individual taxpayers receive a refundable gasoline-price rebate whenever windfall oil profits are taxed, with the largest credits going to households under $150,000 of income ($75,000 for single filers). Married couples filing jointly get 150% of the standard amount.

how_it_helps.text: Imposes a 50% excise tax on each barrel of crude oil extracted or imported by large producers (over 300,000 barrels per day) whenever the quarterly average Brent crude price exceeds its 2025 average, with the threshold adjusted for inflation in later years.

Deposits the tax revenue into a 'Protect Consumers from Gas Hikes Fund' and pays it out as a refundable credit on individual income tax returns, so the money from windfall prices goes back to consumers rather than staying with oil companies.
Phases the rebate down only above $150,000 of income for joint filers and $75,000 for others, and makes the credit fully refundable, so it reaches households that owe little or no income tax.

analysis.who_pays: Very large oil producers and refiners — those extracting or importing more than 300,000 barrels a day — pay the tax on sales above the 2025 baseline price. To the extent companies pass the tax through, drivers could see somewhat higher prices at the pump, offset only when and if rebates are paid.

drawbacks.text: An excise tax on each barrel can be passed through to consumers, so drivers could pay more at the pump before or instead of receiving their rebate — the rebate only arrives after the tax is collected and the Treasury computes it.
The tax only triggers when Brent crude averages above its 2025 level, so consumers get no relief in years when gasoline prices are painfully high but oil has not exceeded the 2025 baseline.

The exemption for companies under 300,000 barrels a day gives smaller producers a competitive advantage over the largest ones, and the rebate amount is uncertain because it depends entirely on how much tax is actually collected each quarter.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: If oil prices spike again the way they did in 2022, the bill would claw back a large share of windfall profits from the biggest oil companies and return the money to households through tax credits, with the phase-out targeting middle- and lower-income filers. The design risks are real: companies may pass part of the tax to consumers at the pump, the rebate lags the price increase, and nothing triggers below the 2025 price baseline. It is a targeted tool for a specific situation — price spikes above a known baseline — rather than general consumer relief.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was introduced and sent to the Senate Finance Committee, where it has sat without a hearing, a markup, or any vote.

narrative.text: Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse and 12 Democratic colleagues plus one independent introduced the bill on March 17, 2026.
The same day, the Senate read it twice and referred it to the Committee on Finance.
No further action appears in the record — no hearing, no committee vote, no floor action.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Large oil companies are better off so far: no windfall tax has been enacted, and any profits above the 2025 baseline remain untaxed. Consumers receive no rebate, though the Congress is still in session and the bill could in theory still move.

sides.party_line_note: All 14 sponsors are Democrats or independents; no Senate Republican has signed on, and the bill sits in a committee chaired by a Republican in a chamber where Republicans hold 55 of 100 seats.

industries.industry: Large oil producers and refiners (over 300,000 barrels per day)
industries.note: The bill takes 50% of the revenue these companies earn on every barrel sold above the 2025 average Brent price, both for oil extracted in the U.S. and oil they import. Because they can pass some of an excise tax through to pump prices, their interest in blocking the bill runs against consumers' interest in the rebate.

industries.industry: Smaller oil producers (under 300,000 barrels per day)
industries.note: The tax applies only to companies extracting or importing more than 300,000 barrels a day, so smaller producers are exempt and gain a price advantage over the largest firms when the tax triggers.

analysis.trajectory: With only 14 of 47 Democratic and independent senators supporting, no Republican cosponsors, and no committee action more than nine months into a two-year Congress, the bill is on the usual path to dying quietly in committee when the session ends in January 2027. A tax increase on oil companies will not reach the floor of a Republican-controlled Senate; the realistic best case is a hearing or a campaign talking point rather than a vote.
